The approach to therapy of other follicular lymphoma differs dramatically in patients with localised or disseminated (advanced) disease.2 In the few patients with limited disease at presentation, ra- diotherapy is potentially curative,1,5-8 with most patients achieving long-term freedom from disease, and low rates of relapse.1 The addition of chemotherapy to radiotherapy does not convincingly prolong remission or improve over- all survival.2,6 Patients who do relapse after therapy should be treated as those with more disseminated disease.2 Even in more advanced disease, which is rarely curable,1,5,7 fol- licular lymphoma may follow a fairly chronic course, with a median survival of 8 or more years4,5,8 although transfor- mation to more aggressive forms may occur.1 Treatment in advanced disease has not been shown to af- fect survival, and a conservative approach of withholding treatment until symptoms require it is considered via- ble.2,3,5,6,8,9 The choice of first-line chemotherapy for ad- vanced disease is controversial.4 Single-agent therapy with chlorambucil or cyclophosphamide, sometimes with a cor- ticosteroid such as prednisone in the initial stages, may be preferred.5,6,9 However, others2 recommend this only for elderly or infirm patients, and then only after rituximab, which is the preferred first-line treatment in these patients. Patients treated with combination chemotherapy tend to have remission earlier but the remissions do not last longer than those achieved more slowly with single-agent thera- py,1 and overall survival has not improved.5,6 Nonetheless, because intensification of chemotherapy has improved re- sponse rates, combination therapy such as CHOP (cyclo- phosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone) has become widely used.5 Some9 consider this regimen too toxic for indolent lymphomas unless rapid tumour de- bulking is required. CVP (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and prednisone) has also been used.4 The addition of ritux- imab to combination chemotherapy has increased overall response rate, response duration, and progression-free sur- vival and hence some recommend rituximab either alone or with other regimens (chemoimmunotherapy) as first- line options; caution is advised in patients with hepatitis B.2 The use of interferon alfa with chemotherapy for first- line treatment has produced conflicting results. However, when interferon alfa was used with anthracycline-contain- ing regimens, improvements in response rate and pro- longed remission were reported;5,9 prolonged survival has not been proven.6 Interferon alfa as maintenance therapy appears to improve disease-free survival, but only if com- plete remission has been obtained with initial chemothera- py.1,5 Overall, a meta-analysis10 of 10 studies found that the ability of interferon alfa to prolong remission duration and survival
